entities.description:
A method with QC target 50 µg/L gives a sample mean of 48.5 µg/L. Does it read systematically low, or could random variation explain the departure? Other questions compare upstream/downstream diclofenac concentrations or growth rates from independent algal cultures, as pictured in [[ref:ex:l6r-m1]]. A hypothesis describes a population parameter or distribution. It does not set our observed test statistic equal to a limit. The reasoning diagram [[ref:ex:l6r-m2]] separates the population claim from the statistic used to check it. In the classical parameter comparisons taught here, H₀ contains equality and H₁ excludes it; this is not a universal definition of every possible hypothesis.

The single tree in [[ref:ex:l6r-m3]] starts with **H₀: μ ≤ L**, where μ is the population mean and L is the reference. **Positive** means rejecting H₀ and claiming an exceedance; **negative** means not rejecting H₀. The thumbnails distinguish true positive, false positive (type I), false negative (type II), and true negative. Non-rejection cannot prove H₀. The three lake hypotheses serve different applications. An equality-only GO policy treats thicker ice as a departure too; non-rejection cannot establish exact equality. Match the burden of evidence to the consequences of an error.

The lake illustration [[ref:ex:l6r-m6]] is a thought experiment about that burden of evidence, not crossing advice. Rule A starts with thickness at or below a hypothetical minimum and goes only after rejection. Rule B starts with thickness at or above the minimum and goes on non-rejection. For the same known-SD Normal measurement model, the decision probabilities in [[ref:ex:l6r-m7]] differ sharply. With four independent readings, population SD 0.5 cm and a 10 cm boundary, sample-mean SE is 0.25 cm. One-sided alpha 5% gives GO thresholds 10.411 cm for A and 9.589 cm for B. At true 9.7 cm, GO occurs about 0.22% versus 67.18%; at true 10.3 cm, about 32.82% versus 99.78%. These compare repeated studies at the same true state, not two analyses producing different physical collapse probabilities from one observed mean. Real ice has local weak spots and other hazards not represented by this model.
entities.label: Population claims, evidence and decisions

entities.description:
Five nitrate results are near ten mg/L and one is 12.5. Preparation errors, contamination, instrument behaviour and genuine pollution events can all produce unusual observations. The investigation picture [[ref:ex:l6r-m59]] begins with keeping the raw value and its sample identity. Check acquisition order, blanks, calibration and preparation records rather than starting with deletion.

Grubbs' statistic [[ref:ex:l6r-m60]] divides the largest absolute deviation from the sample mean by sample SD, calculated from all six original results. Its null is an independent Normal sample, with an alternative concerning one extreme. The two-sided critical construction [[ref:ex:l6r-m61]] accounts for searching the complete sample. For 9.8,9.9,10.0,10.1,10.2,12.5 mg/L, G is about 2.0219 and the 5% cutoff about 1.8871. Compare observed statistic with critical value, just as other tests compare a statistic with a reference rejection region.

Since G exceeds its cutoff, flag **12.5 mg/L** under this model. A flag starts an investigation. Preserve the raw record and document any scientifically justified correction or exclusion. NIST explains the single-outlier reference in [[ref:ex:l6s-sm-grubbs]].

For several suspected outliers, plan a **multiple-outlier procedure**. Generalized ESD [[ref:ex:l6s-sm-esd]] needs an upper bound **r** chosen before testing, an approximately Normal background, and its own adjusted sequential critical values. It calculates successive extreme-deviation statistics and selects the largest qualifying step. Repeated unadjusted Grubbs deletion changes error behaviour; a simple Bonferroni adjustment alone does not resolve adaptive deletion and masking. NIST reports reasonable critical-value approximation from **n ≥ 15**, stronger from **n ≥ 25**. The six-point example above remains a single-outlier illustration.
entities.label: A Grubbs flag starts an investigation

entities.description:
Choose alpha before observing the relevant outcomes. It bounds the procedure's false-rejection probability under H₀ and the sampling model. Lower alpha is not a free improvement: with the same number of observations, variability and true departure, it can increase missed differences. The interactive amoxicillin example [[ref:ex:l6r-m8]] reuses 4000 seeded Normal-sample studies at a fixed true mean 1.4 µg/L versus teaching limit 1 µg/L. Ten independent results and population SD 0.5 µg/L define the model. The readouts distinguish worst-case type I error from simulated type II error.

Degrees of freedom, written **ν** and pronounced nu, describe information remaining after fitting constraints. The residuals add to zero once their mean is fitted. Six independent observations therefore leave **ν = 5** for an SD estimate. Fitting intercept and slope leaves **ν = 4**, as illustrated in [[ref:ex:l6r-m9]]. In these full-rank models, each independently fitted coefficient costs one residual degree of freedom. Other references can use a fractional approximation.

A p-value is a probability conditional on H₀ and the sampling model: a statistic at least as extreme as the one observed, in the planned direction. The upper tail in [[ref:ex:l6r-m10]] counts unusually high results for an exceedance question, with the null boundary used for calibration. Compare p with the alpha chosen in advance. Small p challenges the null model; it is not the probability that H₀ is true, a measurement of effect size, or evidence of causal mechanism.
entities.label: Error levels, degrees of freedom and p-values

entities.description:
The t-test section marker [[ref:ex:l6r-m11]] introduces comparisons of means. A fixed-target comparison differs from comparing two estimated means, shown in [[ref:ex:l6r-m12]]. The **test statistic** [[ref:ex:l6r-m13]] divides the sample mean's departure from its reference by estimated standard error. **SD** describes individual measurement scatter; **SE** describes sampling variation of the mean. Under independent Normal sampling with positive variance and a fixed null mean, the reference has **ν = n − 1**.

The QC experiment [[ref:ex:l6r-m14]] starts at target 50 µg/L, sample mean 48.5 µg/L, sample SD 2 µg/L and six independent preparations. It gives t about −1.837 and two-sided p about 0.126. Changing mean, SD or independent sample size illustrates hypothetical studies, not permission to edit observations or keep collecting until significance appears. The two-sided question counts both extremes.

The separate recovery example [[ref:ex:l6r-m15]] asks whether a minimum population mean recovery of 80% is exceeded. **H₀: μ ≤ 80%; H₁: μ > 80%**. The six synthetic values average **81.5%**. The R-style mimic [[ref:ex:l6r-m16]] reports **t = 3.5032, ν = 5, upper-tail p = 0.008612**. Rejection at 5% supports the population mean being above the illustrative minimum. Individual preparations still vary around that mean. Further reading: NIST one-sample t-test [[ref:ex:l6s-sm-one-t]] and t reference table [[ref:ex:l6s-sm-t-table]].
entities.label: A mean against a fixed target

entities.description:
Sampling identity comes before software choice. The structures in [[ref:ex:l6r-m17]] distinguish independent groups from matched pairs. For independent Normal samples with a justified common variance, the pooled construction [[ref:ex:l6r-m18]] combines sample variances using **residual degrees of freedom as weights**. The river drawing [[ref:ex:l6r-m19]] represents separate upstream and downstream sites. Prior method validation and a homogeneous matrix could support similar within-region measurement variance. Another plausible setting is two randomized groups measured by the same validated assay.

An oxidation batch has a different structure. The before/end bottles in [[ref:ex:l6r-m21]] share a batch, so keep that identity and form one **difference** per independent batch using [[ref:ex:l6r-m20]]. Exact paired-t inference assumes independent Normal differences. The six differences in [[ref:ex:l6r-m22]] include zero and average **2.833 mg/L**. The report [[ref:ex:l6r-m23]] gives **t = 4.0294, ν = 5, two-sided p = 0.01003**. All batches remain; the conclusion concerns the population mean before-minus-end decrease. Time-related competing explanations still matter for causal attribution.

Welch's construction [[ref:ex:l6r-m24]] retains each group's own variance estimate and calibrates an approximate, generally fractional **ν**. The independent sets in [[ref:ex:l6r-m25]] comprise five NIR and six HPLC-MS preparations from one homogeneous reference material. Shared samples measured twice would require pairing. The dot plot [[ref:ex:l6r-m26]] has means **10 and 15 µg/L**. In [[ref:ex:l6r-m27]], NIR minus HPLC-MS is **−5 µg/L**, with **ν ≈ 6.972, p ≈ 0.02089**. Accuracy and method agreement require their own validation. NIST compares the three t constructions in [[ref:ex:l6s-sm-two-t]].
entities.label: Independent groups, shared variance and real pairs

entities.description:
Good scientific practice starts with a population hypothesis, then plans the experiment and analysis before outcomes are known. Check assumptions, apply the prespecified procedure and report the result. Searching endpoints, directions, cutoffs or exclusions until p is small changes the error behaviour. Exploratory analyses can be useful when labelled honestly; they are not replacements for a confirmatory plan.

Consider independent replicate preparations from one water sample and three separate below-limit claims: chloride, bromate and phosphate, each against its own illustrative limit. Each H₀ is at or above the limit and H₁ below. The test-family error criterion here is at least one false below-limit claim. If all three nulls are true and the tests are independent, the chance of no false rejection is 0.95 cubed, or 0.857375. Thus at least one false rejection occurs with probability 0.142625, about 14.26%. Shared sample preparation can make the tests dependent, so that exact rate is an example, not a universal answer. This is not the same decision problem as one joint claim that all analytes pass; a conjunctive pass-only rule has different error logic.

Bonferroni in [[ref:ex:l6r-m28]] divides the chosen 5% test-family level by three, or equivalently multiplies valid raw p-values by three and caps at one. Use only one route. Its union bound permits dependence. The illustrative table [[ref:ex:l6r-m29]] has raw values **0.008, 0.021, 0.200**, adjusted to **0.024, 0.063, 0.600**. Only chloride supports a below-limit claim on this rule. Holm is another prespecified family-wise procedure: sort p, use successive thresholds 0.05/3, 0.05/2 and 0.05, and stop at the first failure. Here its adjusted values are 0.024, 0.042 and 0.200. Choose the procedure in advance. The experiment schematic [[ref:ex:l6s-sm-multi]] makes the three replicate series explicit.
entities.label: Prespecification and a three-claim test-family

entities.description:
The F section marker [[ref:ex:l6r-m30]] opens comparisons of variances. As developed in Level 5, a ratio of independent Normal-sample variances has an F reference when population variances are equal. The **test statistic** [[ref:ex:l6r-m31]] keeps **ν₁ and ν₂** in order. In the precision study [[ref:ex:l6r-m32]], SDs **0.20 and 0.10 mg/L** yield a variance ratio **four**. Six independent preparations per method give **(ν₁, ν₂) = (5, 5)**. The NIST chapter [[ref:ex:l6r-m33]] explains this reference. The report [[ref:ex:l6r-m34]] gives **upper-tail p = 0.07719**: do not reject the equality boundary against greater A variance. Non-rejection cannot prove equal precision. Normality is especially important for this exact reference.

An F-test can instead compare nested models fitted to the same observations. The schematic calibration [[ref:ex:l6r-m35]] contrasts a constant response with adding a concentration slope. Under the shared independent Normal-error model, one added coefficient gives F equal to the square of its corresponding coefficient t statistic. This F question detects either slope direction. It does not require two separate datasets or two unrelated raw variance estimates.

Adding curvature to a straight line is another nested question. The formula [[ref:ex:l6r-m36]] compares error reduction per added coefficient with remaining full-model error per residual degree of freedom. The authored summary in [[ref:ex:l6r-m37]] uses ten standards, two versus three fitted coefficients, and RSS **12 versus 5**; the curves are conceptual. The report [[ref:ex:l6r-m38]] gives **F = 9.8, (ν₁, ν₂) = (1, 7), p = 0.01660**. Reject the zero-curvature coefficient under the shared Normal-error model. Residual checks and validation of the working range remain necessary. NIST describes related conditional coefficient tests in [[ref:ex:l6s-sm-regression]]; for one added coefficient, the nested F equals its squared t statistic.
entities.label: F references for variances and nested calibration fits

entities.description:
The overview [[ref:ex:l6r-m39]] separates a numeric variance question from two questions about counts. For a fixed known target variance, the setup [[ref:ex:l6r-m40]] leads to [[ref:ex:l6r-m41]], an exact Normal-model reference. The six results in [[ref:ex:l6r-m42]] have sample variance **0.024 (mg/L)²**. A known SD target **0.10 mg/L** gives variance **0.010 (mg/L)²**. Multiply by **ν = 5** and divide by the target: **Q = 12**. The report [[ref:ex:l6r-m43]] gives **upper-tail p = 0.03479**, evidence of excess variance at 5%. A separately estimated target requires an analysis including its uncertainty.

For particle categories, Pearson's **test statistic** [[ref:ex:l6r-m44]] adds squared observed-minus-expected count differences divided by expected count. The bars [[ref:ex:l6r-m45]] retain **60 independent particles**: observed **30,20,10**, expected **30,18,12** from fixed shares **50%,30%,20%**. The report [[ref:ex:l6r-m46]] gives **X² = 0.5556, ν = 2, approximate upper-tail p = 0.7575**. Do not reject the mix; this cannot prove its shares. Categories must be exhaustive and mutually exclusive. Fitted shares or sparse expectations require suitable calibration.

For group/damage independence, [[ref:ex:l6r-m47]] obtains expected cells from row and column totals. The synthetic table [[ref:ex:l6r-m48]] has control **8 affected/12 unaffected** and exposure **14/6**. Independence predicts **11 affected and 9 unaffected** in each group of twenty. The report [[ref:ex:l6r-m49]] uses uncorrected Pearson: **X² = 3.6364, ν = 1, approximate upper-tail p = 0.05653**. Do not reject at 5%; this cannot prove independence. Every independent vessel enters one cell. The setup [[ref:ex:l6s-sm-setup]] maps treatment to rows and classification to columns. R's default continuity correction gives a different statistic. Further reading: NIST variance [[ref:ex:l6s-sm-variance]], goodness of fit [[ref:ex:l6s-sm-gof]], and contingency tables [[ref:ex:l6s-sm-independence]].
entities.label: Three distinct chi-square questions

entities.description:
Rank methods use order rather than raw mean distance, but do not remove the need to specify sampling and a null. The independent groups in [[ref:ex:l6r-m50]] contain X values 1,2,2 and Y values 2,3,4. The U statistic [[ref:ex:l6r-m51]] scores an X win one, a tie one half and a loss zero. The grid [[ref:ex:l6r-m52]] gives zero wins, seven losses and two ties: U for X is one. The usual null makes group labels exchangeable under equal distributions. A median-shift interpretation additionally needs the same-shaped location-shift model; differing shapes and detection-limit censoring need care.

The explicit tie-aware reference in [[ref:ex:l6r-m53]] enumerates all twenty assignments of three of the six observations to X, preserving tied observations as distinct units. Six assignments give U at least as far from its null centre 4.5 as the observed value one. Two-sided p is therefore 0.300, and we do not reject at 5%. This convention is declared rather than presenting a no-tie exact table as applicable. The observed tendency for X to be smaller is descriptive, not by itself a significant distributional result.

For paired observations, keep the original pairs. Form one **difference** per pair, then calculate the **rank of abs(diff)** using [[ref:ex:l6r-m54]]. Here abs means absolute value. In [[ref:ex:l6r-m55]], differences **1,−2,3,4,5 µg/L** give **W⁺ = 13** and negative-rank sum **2**. Under the symmetric zero-shift H₀, each independent difference has two equally likely signs. Five choices give **2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 32 patterns**. The total rank sum is **15** and the null centre **7.5**. Three patterns give **W⁺ ≤ 2**, and three give **W⁺ ≥ 13**: **p = 6/32 = 0.1875**, as reported in [[ref:ex:l6r-m56]]. At 5%, do not reject H₀. State zero and tie conventions in software.

Try the reusable compare–score–accumulate interaction [[ref:ex:l6s-sm-score]] before reading the grid. Each click brings one original X/Y pair together and credits the X account. The NIST rank-sum [[ref:ex:l6s-sm-mw]] and signed-rank [[ref:ex:l6s-sm-signed]] pages provide further reading; software statistic orientation and tie conventions can differ. Our declared tie-aware label-permutation calculation remains the reference for this U example.
entities.label: Independent ordering and original paired differences

entities.description:
A **p-value** assesses compatibility with the null model. **Effect magnitude** describes the size of the observed difference. Start with the original units: NIR minus HPLC-MS is **−5 µg/L**. The sampling design limits the scope of inference.

Cohen's d in [[ref:ex:l6r-m57]] divides the independent-group mean difference by pooled within-group descriptive SD. Here **d = −1.677**: NIR reads lower and the mean difference is about **1.68 pooled SDs**. The reference table [[ref:ex:l6s-sm-d-table]] classifies absolute d: below **0.2 negligible**, **0.2 to below 0.5 small**, **0.5 to below 0.8 medium**, and **at least 0.8 large**. Our result is **large** by this convention. These effsize-manual bands describe a standardised magnitude; chemical relevance depends on the application. The mean inference remains Welch.

Cliff's delta in [[ref:ex:l6r-m58]] is the balance of cross-group wins and losses divided by every comparison, including ties. Our earlier grid gives −7/9, about −0.778, indicating X tends lower. Conventional absolute-delta bands are below 0.147 negligible, 0.147 to below 0.33 small, 0.33 to below 0.474 medium, and at least 0.474 large, following the Romano thresholds documented in effsize. They do not set significance or practical-relevance criteria. Comparisons reuse original observations, so uncertainty estimation must respect the independent units, not pretend there are nine independent observations.

entities.description: The normal density has no elementary antiderivative. Its CDF is an antiderivative expressed using the special error function erf. The error function itself is not the normal CDF and is not a probability.

entities.description:

- **z**: Concrete standardized threshold, 2 here (dimensionless).
- **t**: Dimensionless integration variable.
- **P, ≤**: Probability; at or below the threshold.
- **∫, −∞, dt**: Integrate from minus infinity up to z; dt is the increment of t.
- **=, ≈**: Equality and approximate equality.

Inverse function, units and per-result calibration

entities.description:
- **erf(u)**: Error function at dimensionless argument u.
- **u**: Upper integration limit in the definition of erf.
- **t, dt**: Dimensionless integration variable and its infinitesimal increment.
- **∫₀ᵘ**: Integrate from zero to u.
- **e⁻ᵗ²**: Natural exponential with exponent −t².
- **π**: Circle constant.
- **√**: Positive square root.
- **2 / √π**: Normalizing factor in the definition of erf.
- **z / √2**: Scaled standardized threshold used as the erf argument.
- **½, 1, +**: Multiply the grouped expression by one half after adding one.
- **( ), [ ]**: Group the stated operations.

Z, z, density scaling and the variance convention

entities.description: X: random result; x: one value; mu=10.00 mg/L and sigma=0.10 mg/L: independently specified known expectation and positive SD. Standard-normal N(0,1) has mean zero and variance one. Phi lowercase is standard-normal density; f with subscript X is concentration density in L/mg. The factor one over sigma changes density units. Tilde names the law; equality defines/scales the quantities. Subtract, divide and square as shown.

Standardization expresses distance in model SD units

entities.description: An integrable random quantity in an expectation identity.
entities.label: rule U symbol

entities.description: A second integrable random quantity.
entities.label: rule V symbol

entities.description: A random quantity with the moments required by the stated identity.
entities.label: rule Y symbol

entities.description: A placeholder quantity or indexed term in a general mathematical identity.
entities.label: rule a symbol

entities.description: Arithmetic mean of the same finite values a_i.
entities.label: rule abar symbol

entities.description: Insert the two defined differences. Adding them makes the intermediate value appear once with a minus sign and once with a plus sign, so it cancels.
entities.label: Substitute and cancel the intermediate center

entities.description: For n numerical observations, add the values and divide their sum by the positive count n.
entities.label: Arithmetic mean

entities.description: A second placeholder quantity or indexed term.
entities.label: rule b symbol

entities.description: Multiplying a+b by itself gives a², the two equal cross-products ab, and b². Squaring both sides of an equality is a valid implication, not generally a reversible operation without sign information.
entities.label: Binomial square

entities.description: A scalar placeholder; a fixed constant when pulled outside a sum or expectation.
entities.label: rule c symbol

entities.description: If every indexed quantity has expectation m and variance v, the sums of these expectations and variances are nm and nv. This is substitution followed by summing a constant. It says nothing by itself about the variance of a sum: that separate operation may need covariance terms.
entities.label: Substitute common moments in a finite sum

entities.description: Covariance of two random quantities; it measures their joint linear variation.
entities.label: rule cov symbol

entities.description: For U and V with finite second moments, covariance is the expected product of their centered deviations. Positive covariance indicates joint movement in the same direction, negative covariance opposing movement. Independence implies zero covariance, but zero covariance does not generally imply independence.
entities.label: Covariance definition

entities.description: Take expectations of equal integrable random quantities and distribute E over addition. Independence of the two summands is not needed for linearity.
entities.label: Linearity of expectation

entities.description: For integrable random quantities U and V, expectation distributes over their sum. A fixed coefficient c may be taken outside E. Independence is not needed for this rule.
entities.label: Linearity with a fixed multiplier

entities.description: A constant has the same value on every repetition. Its probability-weighted theoretical average is therefore that value. This is not a statement about a random observation that happens to be observed once.
entities.label: Expected value of a constant

entities.description: If integrable random quantities agree with probability one, their expectations agree. Applying E does not require independence. An equality between expectations alone does not recover equality of the random quantities, so the displayed direction is an implication.
entities.label: Expectation preserves equality

entities.description: A constant fixed across repeated samples multiplies the expectation. A random offset such as Δ must not itself be pulled outside E; the fixed count n may be.
entities.label: Factor a fixed constant out of expectation

entities.description: The sample count is fixed and positive. Move 1/n outside expectation and distribute expectation over the finite sum. This needs finite expectations, not independence. It applies to observations and also to squared deviations when their expectations exist.
entities.label: Expected value of a finite average

entities.description: For a fixed finite number of integrable random quantities, apply expectation addition repeatedly. E[ΣY_i] = ΣE[Y_i]. Neither independence nor identical distribution is required. This finite-sum rule alone does not justify interchanging an infinite sum and expectation.
entities.label: Expectation of a finite sum

entities.description: For an integrable random variable Y and fixed real a and b, multiplying the variable by a multiplies its expectation by a; adding b shifts the expectation by b. No independence assumption is needed because the other terms are constants.
entities.label: Expectation under scaling and translation

entities.description: Write a as na/n, subtract a/n and factor out a. The result holds for every real a and positive integer n. This is algebra, not an additional statistical assumption.
entities.label: Factor a common value

entities.description: Split the finite sum over subtraction, count c exactly n times, and substitute Σa_i = n ā. This needs the arithmetic mean of those same values and does not require probability assumptions.
entities.label: Sum distances from a fixed center

entities.description: For independent integrable quantities, the joint distribution factors and the expectation of the product is the product of the expectations. This is not linearity and is generally false for dependent quantities. The independence assumption also ensures integrability of the product under the stated finite absolute moments.
entities.label: Expectation of an independent product

entities.description: The indexed random quantity i in a finite sum.
entities.label: rule indexed Y symbol

entities.description: Subtract c from both sides and read the equality in reverse. This is an equivalent algebraic rearrangement.
entities.label: Subtract the same term

entities.description: Fixed coefficients and a random quantity.
entities.label: Affine expectation

entities.description: Two integrable random quantities.
entities.label: Expectation addition

entities.description: Finite variance and two fixed scalars.
entities.label: Affine variance

entities.description: Expectation and a fixed constant.
entities.label: Constant

entities.description: Both quantities have finite second moments.
entities.label: Variance and covariance

entities.description: A positive count of independent finite-variance quantities.
entities.label: Finite independent sum

entities.description: Independent quantities with finite second moments.
entities.label: Independent pair

entities.description: Finite variance and fixed coefficients.
entities.label: Variance transformation

entities.description: Common expectation of the indexed quantities.
entities.label: rule m symbol

entities.description: Expand each centered difference, distribute the finite sum, and use Σ(a_i−c) = n(ā−c). The two cross-term contributions combine with the last squared shift to leave one negative squared shift. The fitted mean removes a nonnegative term. This is an exact algebraic identity for each realization, not an expectation or an unbiasedness claim.
entities.label: Center squared distances at their arithmetic mean

entities.description: Multiplying the definition of the arithmetic mean by the positive count n gives the sum of the observations.
entities.label: Use the arithmetic mean

entities.description: Divide both sides by the same positive n. Subtract c from both sides to isolate the normalized b term. These are reversible algebraic operations and require no probability assumptions.
entities.label: Divide by a fixed count and rearrange

entities.description: Each observation has expected squared deviation σ² about μ. A finite sum gives nσ². The previously established sample-mean calculation gives E[nΔ²] = σ².
entities.label: Insert the established moment results

entities.description: A factor that does not depend on the index multiplies the entire sum.
entities.label: Factor a constant out of a sum

entities.description: A separate index-independent term; it need not be the square of another coefficient.
entities.label: rule q symbol

entities.description: Subtracting the fitted arithmetic mean from every observation creates one exact sum constraint. It is a deterministic identity, not a claim about expectation.
entities.label: Residuals sum to zero

entities.description: Fixed real scale factor in an affine transformation.
entities.label: rule scale symbol

entities.description: Expand E[(Y−E[Y])²] and use linearity. The middle term is −2(E[Y])² and the constant term is (E[Y])². Rearranging gives E[Y²] = Var(Y)+(E[Y])². A finite second moment is required; independence is not.
entities.label: Second moment and variance

entities.description: Fixed real additive shift in an affine transformation.
entities.label: rule shift symbol

entities.description: Insert an already established equality into the expression, then factor the common value. The statistical premises of the inserted result remain necessary; this algebra does not establish them.
entities.label: Substitute and factor the fixed count

entities.description: Equal values may replace one another in the same expression whenever the operations are defined. The mathematical justification of the substituted value must have been established first; substitution does not prove a statistical premise.
entities.label: Substitute an established equality

entities.description: First distribute the sum over a difference. The second sum repeats c exactly n times and equals nc.
entities.label: Split a sum and count the constant

entities.description: The same value is added once for each of n indices. A quantity can be random across samples and still be constant with respect to i within a given sample.
entities.label: Sum a constant

entities.description: Add the left sides and the right sides of equalities that hold at every index. This gives a consequence; the summed equality alone does not recover every individual equality.
entities.label: Sum indexed equalities

entities.description: A finite sum distributes over addition. No independence or probability assumption is needed.
entities.label: Linearity of a finite sum

entities.description: Use linearity for each of the three summands and move the index-independent coefficient c outside the middle sum. The last sum is not simplified yet.
entities.label: Distribute the sum and factor the cross term

entities.description: Common finite variance of the indexed quantities.
entities.label: rule v symbol

entities.description: For a fixed real constant c, E[c] = c, so c−E[c] = 0 on every outcome. Its expected squared centered deviation is therefore zero.
entities.label: Variance of a constant

entities.description: For two random quantities with finite second moments, expand the squared centered sum. The expected cross product is the covariance. Positive covariance increases the variance of the sum; negative covariance decreases it. Independence is not needed for this identity.
entities.label: Variance-covariance identity

entities.description: For a random variable with finite second moment, variance is the expected squared distance from its expectation.
entities.label: Variance is an expected squared deviation

entities.description: Mutual independence makes every cross covariance zero. The variance of the finite sum then equals the sum of its variances. For two variables this reduces to Var(U+V) = Var(U)+Var(V). Standard deviations are not directly additive.
entities.label: Variance of a finite independent sum

entities.description: Combine translation invariance with the squared scaling factor. For fixed a and b and finite variance, Var(aY+b) = a² Var(Y). Unlike expectation, variance does not acquire an additive b term.
entities.label: Variance under scaling and translation

entities.description: Variance squares the centered distance. Replacing Y by cY multiplies every centered distance by c and its square by c². Consequently variance is multiplied by c², not by c. The standard deviation is multiplied by the absolute value of c.
entities.label: Variance under scaling

entities.description: Adding a fixed c moves the random quantity and its expectation by the same amount. Their difference is unchanged, so the variance is unchanged. This does not hold for adding an arbitrary random quantity.
entities.label: Variance under translation

entities.description: For a finite collection with finite second moments, the variance-covariance identity includes all pairwise cross covariances. When each is zero, only the individual variances remain. Independence is sufficient for this result but pairwise zero covariance is enough.
entities.label: Variance of a pairwise uncorrelated sum

entities.description: The histograms use successive prefixes of one simulated Normal sequence with expectation 10.00 mg/L and SD 0.10 mg/L. Bin edges and the generating model remain fixed.
entities.label: More draws from one assumed stable normal method

entities.description:
- **Choose the sample size.** `c` lists the allowed result counts. `%in%` checks whether `M` belongs to that list, and `stopifnot` enforces this choice.
- **Prepare the simulation.** `numeric` allocates the result vector; `seq_len` supplies the iteration indices.
- **Generate reproducible results.** The Park–Miller recurrence updates an integer-valued state using multiplication and the remainder operator `%%`. `qnorm` transforms the resulting uniform fractions into standard-normal values. Scaling and shifting set the stated SD and mean.
- **Build the histogram.** `seq` creates fixed bin edges. `hist` computes and draws density bins whose left edges belong to the bin.
- **Check the counts.** `sum` totals the bin counts; `cat` reports that total alongside `M` so that count conservation can be checked.
entities.label: R functions and the deterministic stream

entities.description:
- **$j$**: Group index $A$ or $B$.
- **$ν_j$**: Group $j$'s sample count minus one, giving its degrees of freedom.
- **$S_j^2$**: Random sample variance about group $j$'s fitted mean ($\mathrm{(mg/L)^2}$).
- **$σ_j^2$**: Positive true variance of group $j$ ($\mathrm{(mg/L)^2}$).
- **$Q_j$**: Scaled sample variance, $\frac{ν_j S_j^2}{σ_j^2}$ (dimensionless).
- **$F$**: Resulting dimensionless random ratio; also the name of its reference distribution.
- **$()^2, /, =, ∼$**: Variance from squaring an SD; division; equality; follows the named distribution.
- **Comma**: Orders distribution parameters: numerator B degrees of freedom, then denominator A.

The Normal samples and groups are independent, making $Q_A$ and $Q_B$ independent chi-square variables. Both degrees of freedom are five here. Equal true variances cancel; otherwise normalize the sample-variance ratio by the true $B/A$ variance ratio.
entities.label: tf f law symbol
Equal true variances give a reference for the sample ratio

entities.description:

- **$s_A^2$**: Observed variance in group A, $0.010\,\mathrm{(mg/L)^2}$.
- **B, A**: Group subscripts specifying the prespecified numerator and denominator.
- **², /, =**: Squaring an SD to obtain variance, division and equality.

Each group contains six independent results, with independent groups. Each variance uses that group's fitted mean and divisor five. Concentration units cancel in B/A; the group order is fixed before inspecting the data.

entities.description: Residuals sum to zero: Σᵢ(Xᵢ − X̄) = 0. Only n − 1 residuals are free; SS_res is their sum of squares.

entities.description: Divide SS_res by n − 1: E[s²] = σ². Division by n instead gives (n − 1)σ²/n on average.

entities.description: The total sum of squares about the population mean equals the residual sum of squares about the sample mean plus n times the squared distance between the two means. Taking expectations leaves n minus one times population variance for residuals.

entities.description:

- **Z**: Standardized random variable, with mean zero and variance one under the Normal model.

- **N, ∼**: Normal distribution, parameterized by mean and variance; follows that distribution.

entities.label: Intermediate precision

entities.description: Scenario: different laboratories analyze the same homogeneous QC material using a specified procedure. Their results assess between-laboratory conditions. These labels do not imply a universal ordering of SDs.

entities.description: Inject one prepared vial three times. These technical replicates assess instrumental variation, not new preparation or field sampling. Shared drift may still make the readings dependent.

entities.description: Xᵢ: observation i; μ: population mean; dᵢ = Xᵢ − X̄; Δ = X̄ − μ. n > 1: count; Σ: sum from i = 1 to n.
entities.label: Residuals and offset

entities.description: E: repeated-sampling expectation; σ²: population variance; MSDₙ: residual sum of squares divided by n. Here σ² = 5 (mg/L)².
entities.label: The variance target

entities.description: Subtract E(nΔ²) = σ² from nσ². Assumptions: independent identical sampling, finite variance. Normality is not needed.
entities.label: Apply the preceding result

entities.description: Population variance: 5 (mg/L)². Average MSD is lower, especially for small samples.
entities.label: vv ep1

entities.description: 5,000 independent samples per size; seed 1903. These averages approximate expectations.
entities.label: vv ep2

entities.description: Bias concerns expectation, not each realization. Why does fitting the mean reduce squared deviations?
entities.label: vv ep3

entities.description: X̄: random sample mean; x̄: realized value. μ: population mean; σ²: finite population variance; n > 1: sample size.
entities.label: Random mean, fixed population

entities.description: E: expectation; Var: variance; Δ = X̄ − μ. E(Δ²) = Var(X̄). Assumptions: independent, identically distributed observations. Normality is not required.
entities.label: Expected squared shift

entities.description: Δ = X̄ − μ. Because E(X̄) = μ, E(Δ²) = Var(X̄). Multiply by fixed n. Normality is not required.
entities.label: The needed auxiliary result

entities.description: Prepared instructor demonstration: interpret the estimates, not the R programming.
entities.label: vv intro point

entities.description: Each point averages MSD estimates over 5,000 independent Normal samples at the stated size, using seed 1903. The averages fall below the model variance of 5 (mg/L) squared. They are finite approximations, not exact expectations.
entities.label: Many Repetitions, Lower Average MSD

entities.description: Prepared demonstration: average 5,000 independent samples per size, then compare with the known variance.
entities.label: vv mc point

entities.description: Population variance
entities.label: vv mc ref line

entities.description: Independent normal observations. Mean μ = 10 mg/L; variance σ² = 5 (mg/L)²; SD σ = √5 mg/L.
entities.label: A known population

entities.description: Population variance
entities.label: vv ref line

entities.description: Theory gives the expectation curve. Finite Monte Carlo averages approximate it with simulation variation.
entities.label: vv rp1

entities.description: n = 2, 3, 5, 10, 25, 50, 100. Fit each sample mean, then calculate MSD with divisor n. Seed 1901.
entities.label: Five fresh samples at each size

entities.description: 495 independent samples; seed 1902. Each point is one MSD, not a connected trajectory.
entities.label: Five Samples at Every Size

entities.description: The five realizations per size illustrate sampling fluctuation. Estimator bias is assessed through its repeated-sampling expectation.
entities.label: vv scatter point

entities.description: Xᵢ: observation i; μ: population mean; dᵢ: residual about X̄. n: count; i: index; Σ: sum from 1 to n.
entities.label: Values and sums

entities.description: Δ = X̄ − μ is shared by every observation. Superscript 2 means square. Keep the residual, cross and offset terms.
entities.label: One common shift

entities.description: The solid curve is the derived expectation; points are seeded Monte Carlo averages. The dashed line is the true population variance.
entities.label: Theory and Monte Carlo

entities.description: s²: sample variance; dᵢ: observation i minus its fitted mean; n > 1: count; Σ: sum over i = 1 to n.
entities.label: Sample variance

entities.description: E: expectation; σ²: population variance. The numerator averages (n−1)σ², so division by n−1 targets σ². Sampling must be iid with finite variance.
entities.label: Remove average bias

entities.description: Expectation explains unbiased variance estimation. Residual degrees of freedom describe constraints. The square root s is not automatically unbiased.
entities.label: Keep the arguments separate

entities.description: Xᵢ: random observation i; μ: population mean; dᵢ: residual about X̄; Δ: X̄ − μ. i indexes observations.
entities.label: Symbols

entities.description: Superscript 2 means square. The two cross-products give 2Δdᵢ. Every term has unit (mg/L)².
entities.label: Square all terms

entities.description: dᵢ = Xᵢ − X̄: residual of observation i. Σ sums from 1 to n. Since Σdᵢ = 0, the cross term is zero.
entities.label: The cross term vanishes

entities.description: Δ = X̄ − μ; μ: population mean; n: count. The shared squared shift occurs n times. Superscript 2 means square.
entities.label: The offset remains

entities.description: The same quantity can take different values for different reasons. In our UV/Vis experiment we choose concentrations. In the lake we observe them.
entities.label: why values differ intro

entities.description: Some differences are created by design. Others arise in the sampled system or measurement process. A variable's role depends on the study design.
entities.label: why values differ takeaway

entities.description: Fünf Wiederholbestimmungen einer Koffeinprobe werden mit Mittelwert und Bessel-korrigierter Stichprobenstandardabweichung ausgewertet. Die Streuung beschreibt die Präzision unter den angegebenen Wiederholbedingungen; ohne Referenzwert oder Wiederfindung wird keine Richtigkeit abgeleitet.
entities.label: caffeine determination

entities.description: In a UV/Vis calibration series, analyte concentration is deliberately changed between standards and therefore acts as the independent variable. Absorbance is the measured dependent response. The measurement wavelength is held at 540 nm and is therefore a constant within this experiment.
entities.label: UV/Vis calibration roles

entities.description: Illustrative concentrations in mg/L: samples A, B and C; nitrate and phosphate.
entities.label: worked example concentration value shapes

entities.description: A measured concentration may be modeled as a continuous random variable over the physically admissible range when the measurement model treats concentration as continuously valued.
entities.label: concentration as a continuous random variable

entities.description: For a fixed sampled volume and counting protocol, the observed number of colonies is integer-valued and can be modeled as a discrete random variable.
entities.label: colony count as a discrete random variable

entities.description: A traveler covers two equal-distance sections at 10 m/s and 2 m/s. Total distance divided by total travel time gives 10/3 m/s ≈ 3.33 m/s, equal to the harmonic mean of the two speeds.
entities.label: average speed over equal-distance sections

entities.description: Target unit: µg/L. Table A Fe is already 0.1, 0.2 and 0.3 µg/L and therefore remains 0.1, 0.2 and 0.3 µg/L. Table A Cu values 0.2, 0.3 and 0.4 mg/L become 200, 300 and 400 µg/L. Table B Fe values 0.0003, 0.0007 and 0.0011 mg/L become 0.3, 0.7 and 1.1 µg/L. Table B Cu values 0.15, 0.25 and 0.335 mg/L become 150, 250 and 335 µg/L.
entities.label: corrected concentration-unit harmonization example

entities.description: In a chromatographic calibration, standard concentration is deliberately varied and acts as the independent variable, while peak area is the dependent response. The nominal injection-volume setting is kept at 5 µL and is a constant within this calibration.
entities.label: chromatographic calibration roles

entities.description: Two equal successive periods have multiplicative factors 2 and 8. Their geometric mean is 4, and applying factor 4 in each period preserves the total factor: 4 × 4 = 2 × 8 = 16.
entities.label: equivalent multiplicative growth factor

entities.description: Fünf pH-Werte werden über Mittelwert, Abweichungen, Quadratsumme und Stichprobenstandardabweichung ausgewertet.
entities.label: repeated pH measurement

entities.description: For 2.1, 2.3, 2.0, 2.2 and 45.0 NTU, the arithmetic mean is 10.72 NTU and the median is 2.2 NTU. The example illustrates the greater resistance of the median to one extreme observation; which summary is scientifically preferable still depends on the question being asked.
entities.label: turbidity data with one extreme observation

entities.description: Illustrative analytical data: a concentration of 2.55 mg/L, a replicate count of 3, an impedance of 2 + 3i ohms, a sample class of lake and a passed quality check.
entities.label: worked example variable value types

entities.description: When nitrate concentrations are compared between sampling sites, sampling site can act as an independent explanatory or grouping variable and nitrate concentration as the dependent response, while the analytical protocol keeps the nominal aliquot volume at 10.0 mL as a constant. Because site is observed rather than experimentally manipulated, this role assignment alone does not establish a causal effect of site.
entities.label: environmental sampling roles

entities.description: sample arithmetic mean
entities.label: xbar symbol

entities.description: i-th observed value
entities.label: xi symbol

entities.description: Using the sample mean and the same sample-standard-deviation convention gives transformed sample values with sample mean 0 and sample standard deviation 1 when s is non-zero. Using population parameters gives population mean 0 and population standard deviation 1 when sigma is non-zero. The conventions must not be mixed silently.
entities.label: z score convention interpretation

entities.description: Ordinary mean-and-standard-deviation z-score standardization is not robust to outliers: extreme observations can affect both the centering mean and the scaling standard deviation.
entities.label: z score outlier sensitivity interpretation
